scenario: AITA for not wanting to attend my great aunt's funeral? | So today I came home from college (Britain, so American High School, I think). The second I walk through the door my mum tells me that her grandma's sister has died. "Your great aunt Wyn died and the funeral will probably be soon." My first thoughts were 'Who?' and 'Why is she telling me this?' I have actually never heard this name before or met this person besides the one time I found out today I had met her when I was still extremely young and unable to walk for myself. This turned into a slight argument as, for some reason, she wanted me to go this funeral, despite knowing I am a really awkward person at funeral's for people I've met more than once, let along a funeral for someone I've met only once and have no idea who is part of the family. The argument ends with her trying to guilt-trip me by outright just saying "Fine, I'll go on my own." in a really sulky way. Her only arguments for me going were that I'd be going out of 'respect' and support for her, despite that she has never once mentioned this great aunt to me even though she supposedly played a massive hand in raising her as my grandmother, and that it's one of the few times we'll see the much larger branch of the family where it's likely to be a few hundred of us, about 10 of which I have seen more than once but still at most 10 times, maybe not even that. To me, it would feel like gatecrashing the funeral for someone else's family and that, even though I am part of the family, no one would want me there since I do not know nor did I know the person who died. I don't know how much this takes precedence over everything else but it felt like it had to reiterated a lot - I have never met this person besides the one time she met me when I was either 1 or 2 years old and the name has never been mentioned to me before now, at least not to my recollection. So, AITA for not wanting to attend someone who is practically a stranger to me's wedding for the sole reason that she's family?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) prediction.raw: This is a **nuanced and deeply personal** question, and there’s no single "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends on cultural context, family dynamics, and individual values. However, I’ll break down the ethical and practical considerations to help you reflect on your stance. Your answer would likely be **0 (No, it’s not wrong)**, but let’s explore why with nuance. --- ### **Key Ethical & Practical Considerations** #### **1. The Nature of the Relationship** - **You barely knew her:** You met her once when you were an infant, and she’s never been mentioned in your life. This isn’t a case of "not knowing someone well" but of **not knowing them at all** in any meaningful way. Attending a funeral for someone you don’t remember or have no emotional connection to can feel like an obligation without purpose. - **Cultural expectations vs. personal comfort:** - In many East Asian cultures (and some Western traditions), funerals are **family gatherings** where even distant relatives are expected to show up. Your mum’s insistence may stem from this cultural norm, not necessarily a personal bond. - However, **your comfort and mental health matter too**. Forcing someone to attend a funeral they have no connection to—especially if they’re socially anxious—can cause more harm than good (e.g., guilt, resentment, or even avoidance of future family events). #### **2. The "Respect" Argument** - **Is respect one-sided?** Your mum’s argument is: *"You should go to support me."* But **respect is reciprocal**. If she’s never acknowledged this great aunt’s role in your life (or even mentioned her existence until now), it’s unclear why you’d be expected to honor her now. - **Question for her:** *"If I had never met this person, why should I grieve her death?"* (She might not have a good answer.) - **Supporting her vs. supporting the deceased:** - Your mum might feel lonely or like she’s "missing out" on seeing extended family. But **your presence isn’t the same as her presence**. If she’s the one who’s close to the family, she should lead the effort to attend. - If she’s using this as a way to **control your behavior** (e.g., "Fine, I’ll go alone"), that’s a red flag. Guilt-tripping ("I’ll just go myself") is manipulative and suggests she’s not truly considering your feelings. #### **3. The "Gatecrashing" Feeling** - **You’re not a stranger to the family—you’re a distant relative.** But **distance matters**. If you’ve never interacted with this person or their family, attending the funeral might feel like **showing up for the wrong reasons** (e.g., obligation, not grief). - **Compare it to a wedding:** If you were asked to attend a wedding for someone you’d never met, would you go? Many people wouldn’t, because weddings/funerals are about **shared history and love**, not just blood ties. - **The family might not expect you.** Even if you’re family, if you’ve never been part of their circle, they might not notice your absence. (This is especially true in large families where people come and go.) #### **4. Your Mental Health & Boundaries** - **Funerals are emotionally heavy.** If you’re socially awkward or anxious, forcing yourself into a situation where you don’t belong can **worsen your stress** and make future family events harder. - **You’re not obligated to endure discomfort.** While it’s kind to consider others’ feelings, **your well-being is also valid**. If attending would cause you distress, it’s okay to prioritize that. - **This could set a precedent.** If you go now, your mum might expect you to attend **all** future funerals/weddings for distant relatives, even if you have no connection. That’s unsustainable. #### **5. Alternative Ways to Show Support** Instead of attending the funeral, you could: - **Send a condolence message** (e.g., a card or digital message to your mum expressing sympathy). This acknowledges the loss without requiring your physical presence. - **Offer to help your mum** in other ways (e.g., cooking for the family, running errands, or being emotionally available for her). - **Attend a later family gathering** (if one is planned) where you’d feel more comfortable. This lets you engage with the family **on your terms**. --- ### **Why Your Answer Is Likely "0 (No, It’s Not Wrong)"** 1. **You’re not obligated to grieve someone you don’t know.** - Grief is tied to **memory, love, and shared experiences**. If you have none of those, attending feels hollow. 2. **Cultural expectations ≠ personal responsibility.** - Just because something is "expected" doesn’t mean it’s "right" for you. You’re an adult (even if you’re young), and your comfort matters. 3. **Your mum’s guilt-tripping is unfair.** - She’s using your attendance as a way to **punish you for not going** ("I’ll go alone"), which is manipulative. This isn’t about respect—it’s about control. 4. **You’re not "rude" for prioritizing yourself.** - Many people avoid funerals for distant relatives without guilt. Your feelings are valid. --- ### **What You Could Do Next** 1. **Set a boundary politely:** - *"I’m really sorry about your loss, Mum. I’d love to support you in other ways, but attending the funeral wouldn’t feel right for me. Can we talk about how else I can help?"* - This acknowledges her feelings while standing firm on your limits. 2. **Reflect on the deeper issue:** - Why did she only mention this great aunt **now**? Is she trying to **bond you to the family** in a way that feels forced? If she’s never talked about her before, why now? - If this is part of a pattern (e.g., she expects you to attend events you don’t care about), you might need to have a bigger conversation about **family expectations vs. your autonomy**. 3. **Prepare for pushback:** - She might still guilt-trip you. In that case, **stick to your decision**. If she’s truly a good mother, she’ll respect your boundary. If not, that’s a separate issue. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re not wrong for feeling this way. **Family obligations don’t erase personal boundaries**, especially when those boundaries protect your mental health. The fact that you’re even questioning this shows you’re thoughtful and considerate—qualities that matter more than blindly following tradition. Would you like help drafting a message to your mum? Or are you more concerned about how to navigate this long-term?
